items.title: Primark sales slip ahead of ABF exit in ‘challenging’ backdrop
items.summary: Primark has seen its sales slip as its owner, Associated British Foods, races to shape up the fast-fashion retailer ahead of its exit from the group next year.  Like-for-like sales at the retailer slipped by 2.6 per cent in the year to September, dragged down by “weak” consumer confidence and less advanced turnaround efforts in [...]
items.body:
Primark sales slip ahead of ABF exit in ‘challenging’ backdrop
Primark has seen its sales slip as its owner, Associated British Foods, races to shape up the fast-fashion retailer ahead of its exit from the group next year.
Like-for-like sales at the retailer slipped by 2.6 per cent in the year to September, dragged down by “weak” consumer confidence and less advanced turnaround efforts in its European market.
Consumer giant ABF is racing to put Primark on a solid footing ahead of its demerger in December next year but told shareholders on Tuesday that these efforts are coming up against a “challenging consumer market”.
ABF’s overall performance was dragged down by a heavy loss at its sugar arm, as the FTSE 100 group slipped to a pre-tax profit of £1.3bn, 10 per cent lower than last year.
Primark’s drop in like-for-like sales was blamed on a 4.7 per cent dip in Continental Europe. This is the retailer’s biggest market, accounting for 47 per cent of its sales.
The group said its sales declined in this market because “consumer sentiment remained weak and we are at an earlier stage in our commercial recovery and in the development of our capabilities in brand, marketing and digital capabilities”.
Primark’s sales in the UK and Ireland grew by 0.5 per cent across the year, though its like-for-like takings declined by 0.1 per cent in the second half, suggesting a drop-off in consumer spending.
The group is working to improve Primark’s womenswear offering and its presence in the UK, it said. In September, the retailer announced it will roll out home delivery for the first time.
Eoin Tonge, chief executive of Primark, said on Tuesday that the retailer aims to roll out home delivery by the end of next year. He said: “After years of review, we feel very confident that it’s time to now target profitable growth in this channel.”
Primark’s boss added that the retailer is aiming to introduce more fashionable products to win over more customers. He said: “We’ve strengthened our core womenswear fashion offer, bringing more elevated contemporary style to the mat. All designed to challenge the perceptions of what affordable fashion can look and feel like.”
ABF told shareholders that Primark has come up against a “challenging consumer environment in most markets”. But the group said its franchise stores in the Middle East, which include locations like Dubai and Bahrain, are performing ahead of expectations.
Hot weather hits tea sales
Chief executive George Weston said the group’s food operations were “impacted by US consumer weakness in certain categories and lower European sugar prices”.
ABF’s sugar arm, which has been at the centre of the group’s woes in recent months, slumped to an adjusted operating loss of £47m due to lower sugar prices.
The group said hot weather in the UK and France weighed on sales in its Twinings tea businesses, though it has attempted to boost takings with a new cold tea range in Australia.
Across ABF’s grocer businesses, its revenue climbed by three per cent in the year to £4.2bn, as adjusted operating profit slipped by 10 per cent to £383m.
Weston said the headline profit dip “masked encouraging growth across a number of brands and businesses, supported by continued investment in product innovation, marketing and targeted acquisitions”.
The group recently bought bakery giant Hovis, and said it expects to make “significant cost synergies” as it merges this company with its own Allied Bakeries division.
Analysts at stock broker RBC said ABF’s update was “cautious on consumer sentiment” as Primark faces a “tougher macro and competitive backdrop in major markets, particularly outside the UK”.
ABF’s majority shareholder is Wittington Investments, a trust controlled by the billionaire Weston family. Last month, the firm behind the Westons’s Canadian business interests bought high street giant Boots for £6.7bn.
Shares in ABF lost 2.6 per cent to 1,891.5p in early trading.

items.title: Poundland staff could be out of work for years if retailer collapses, founder says
items.summary: Steve Smith calls on owners to accept proposed buyout as 12,000 staff face uncertain future in run-up to Christmas The founder of Poundland has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal. Steve Smith, who set up the firm with a store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, said: “Once these jobs are lost, they are lost” from Britain’s struggling high streets. His warning comes as the chain’s 12,000 employees face uncertainty over their future in the run-up to Christmas. Continue reading...
items.body:
The founder of Poundland has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal.
Steve Smith, who set up the firm with a store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, said: “Once these jobs are lost, they are lost” from Britain’s struggling high streets. His warning comes as the chain’s 12,000 employees face uncertainty over their future in the run-up to Christmas.
Poundland’s future hangs in the balance after the retailer, which is controlled by the US restructuring specialist Gordon Brothers, filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.
The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors until 12 November while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the likelihood of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers have held back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.
Poundland’s management is scheduled to meet Kate Dearden, the minister for the future of work, on Wednesday as political pressure mounts on Gordon Brothers to accept an offer from Northern Ireland’s Martin Property Group rather than calling in administrators to break up the retailer.
The restructuring firm is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer.
Smith – who sold his final shares in Poundland for £250m in 2006 – said he was prepared to support that offer but Martin Property Group did not need his cash.
“It was my baby,” he said, adding that he had put in an offer when Poundland was first put up for sale but had not heard back and it was too late to now launch his own bid.
“If they have got offers on the table, why is Gordon Brothers not taking it and saving all these people? Retail is hard out there and if these people lose their job it could be a couple of years before they get jobs again. They work week to week and need their wages,” Smith said.
“It is not just 12,000 jobs. Poundland has more than 2,000 suppliers, some only deal with Poundland and some employ hundreds of people.”
He suggested that as many as 30,000 jobs could be at risk in Poundland’s supply chain, stores and at other affected businesses on high streets around the country.
“Poundland brings in 4 million to 5 million customers every week to towns and shopping centres and retail neighbours are going to suffer as well,” Smith said.
“Now it has been restructured and is turning a corner and starting to do well.”
It is understood that talks continue about a potential deal under which Martin Property Group has offered about £7.5m up front and the same again in deferred payments over the next two years.
That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood.
This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, a former owner of Poundland that holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News.
Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

items.title: Miniso gets physical in London as Currys taps TikTok Shop: the biggest retail technology stories from October
items.summary: October is done and dusted, November is up and running, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful month for the retail technology space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from October, including Morrisons, Instacart, DoorDash, Holland & Barrett, Ikea UK, Duvo, Muffato G
items.body:
October is done and dusted, November is up and running, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful month for the retail technology space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from October, including Morrisons, Instacart, DoorDash, Holland & Barrett, Ikea UK, Duvo, Muffato Group, Sensei, Enactor, Jysk, and StrongPoint.
1. Holland & Barrett announces €17.5 million investment across digital and retail fulfilment in Ireland
UK health and wellness retailer, Holland and Barrett, has announced a €17.5 million investment across digital and retail fulfilment in Ireland over the next three years.
From 1st November, fulfilment of its Irish online orders will move from the UK to Ireland through an expanded three-year partnership with Kildare-based Road Truck Services (RTS), building on an eight-year relationship spanning import, customs, warehousing and distribution.
The move will see €8.2 million invested in a new digital fulfilment model, alongside €9.3 million relating to existing retail fulfilment operations with RTS, bringing the total investment to €17.5 million over the next three years.
Around €1.5 million of additional stock will be held locally, bringing Holland & Barrett’s total Irish stockholding to approximately €4.7 million. Around 328,000 orders and 1.8 million units are expected to flow through the Irish logistics network each year.
The expanded partnership is also expected to support around 20 additional RTS roles, alongside agency support during peak periods and a further 6-10 indirect roles, with recruitment focused on Kildare town and surrounding areas.
For customers, the move will mean greater choices on online orders from 1st November, with the existing 5kg weight limit lifted and additional products from 34 Irish brands available online. Next-day delivery is planned to launch from 1st December.
The investment comes as Holland & Barrett grows its presence in Ireland. Approximately 2.8 million customers shopped with the business over the past year, and it now operates 70 stores and employs 419 colleagues across the country.
2. Morrisons bins Instacart AI powered Caper Carts trial amid DoorDash acquisition talks
In July, we reported that Morrisons had launched Instacart’s Caper Cart smart trolleys at a Preston supermarket, marking North American firm Instacart’s first retail partnership in the UK for its AI powered solution.
Three months later, however, the retailer is pulling the trial as DoorDash gets set to acquire Instacart in a deal that values the grocery technology specialist at around $17 billion.
Separately, Instacart said in a regulatory filing that it would wind down its Caper Cart business by the end of the second quarter of 2027, expecting pre-tax charges of $55 million to $80 million related to the move.
The plan is to reinvest any savings into strategic growth initiatives, which includes other in-store solutions like smart price tags and computer vision technology to help grocers track in-store inventory.
Responding to the news, retail analyst Steve Dresser said on LinkedIn: "Not one to mock innovation, it's vital. But this was always overplayed and seemed to be a chance for people to get their name in lights, rather than a meaningful trial to scale."
3. Quorso and VoCoVo among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Retailer/Technology Supplier Relationship finalists
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Best Retailer/Technology Supplier Relationship category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! Our winners will be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
4. Ikea stumps up £31.5 million as it looks to make UK fulfilment more efficient and reduce packaging waste
Ikea UK is investing £31.5 million across its Peterborough and Doncaster customer distribution centres (CDC) as the retailer aims to make online fulfilment more efficient and sustainable.
In Peterborough, new technology is packaging customer orders to size and reducing material usage by up to 30%, by preventing waste from oversized boxes and filling paper. In Doncaster, Ikea is trialling a new regional fulfilment capability, serving customers in the north and Scotland from a closer location to them.
The investments will strengthen Ikea’s UK fulfilment network as online sales account for 43.3% of total UK sales in financial year 2026. It is investing £30 million in new technology for its Peterborough CDC, with the upgrades taking place over a two-year period. As part of this, it has launched new PackSize technology to prevent waste from oversized cardboard boxes and filling materials by packaging customer orders to size. On average, the technology reduces material usage by up to 30% and void fill by up to 60%.
The technology is expected to increase the share of parcels processed through automation at the Peterborough CDC from 47% today to 75% in 2027, helping the fulfilment team prepare orders for delivery more efficiently. These additional orders would otherwise have been packaged by manually creating a packing carton which includes having to measure the article then creating the cartons to fit the order. Three drones and nests were introduced at the site in January to support inventory management. They scan each aisle in short cycles, helping Ikea to keep stock in the right place and meet customer demand.
Ikea is investing £1.5 million in trialling a new fulfilment capability at its Doncaster CDC. The site now fulfils orders for customers in the Gateshead, Edinburgh and Glasgow areas, with plans for Sheffield to follow. By fulfilling these orders from Doncaster rather than Peterborough, Ikea expects to reduce emissions from delivery journeys by an estimated 280 tonnes of CO2 annually. The new capability has created an additional 80 jobs at the Doncaster site.
5. Sensei looks to take retail intelligence beyond the store checkout as it teams with Brazil’s Muffato Group
Sensei has deployed its technology in a new Muffato Go store in Curitiba, Brazil. This has been developed in partnership with supermarket specialist Grupo Muffato.
While Sensei first became known for its autonomous store technology, it says that the intelligence behind those stores has always been designed to address a broader challenge: giving physical retail the ability and the data to understand and automate its own operations in real-time.
The new Muffato Go, according to those involved, will put that capability into practice, showing how the same underlying technology can improve shelf availability, detect losses, automate checkout, manage fresh products and support online order fulfillment.
Headquartered in Portugal and operating across Europe and Brazil, Sensei has deployed its technology in more than 100 autonomous points of sale, including the world's largest autonomous store, opened in Leiria, Portugal, in 2025.
“The new Muffato Go shows what AI can already do in a physical store. Shoppers get a faster, simpler way to buy, but that is only the visible part. Our models recognise products and shopper interactions as they happen, and store teams get the right task at the right time," says Vasco Portugal, CEO and Co-founder at Sensei.
"The real value is turning what happens in the store into intelligence that supports the entire business, from the shop floor to the head office. That is what we mean by Conscious Spaces: physical spaces that see, understand and act."
6. Enactor powered unified commerce Jysk roll-out progresses at pace across retailer's UK and Ireland stores
Danish home furnishing retailer Jysk reports that the first of its UK and Ireland stores are now live with its Enactor powered unified commerce platform.
In a LinkedIn post, Patrick Gretsch, Retail Operations Expert at Jysk, said: "Two more countries have taken their first steps towards a new way of working, with the first stores in the UK and Ireland now successfully running on our unified commerce platform."
"I had the pleasure of joining the team at our Sallynoggin store in Ireland to experience one of these first transitions firsthand. What stood out was the excellent preparation and collaboration across all departments involved. The result? A smooth and efficient changeover, completed while the store remained open and continued serving customers."
He added: "And this is just the beginning. The roll-out is progressing at pace, with all Jysk stores in both countries expected to be running on the new platform by mid-November. So, what does this mean for our colleagues and customers? For our store teams, unified commerce means simpler processes and new opportunities to serve customers directly on the shop floor. With mobile PoS, colleagues can process payments right where the customer interaction takes place, making the shopping experience more convenient and personal."
"For our customers, it opens the door to additional services. They can, for example, order products in a store and have them delivered directly coming from our warehouse straight to their doorstep. This is what makes unified commerce so exciting: it’s not just about introducing a new platform. It’s about improving the way we work and creating new opportunities to serve our customers."
7. Morrisons partners with StrongPoint ALS and VoCoVo on Click & Collect pilot at Skipton store
Morrisons has launched a pilot of StrongPoint ALS’s temperature controlled Click & Collect lockers at the retailer’s Skipton store in North Yorkshire.
The aim here is to provide a convenient and flexible way to collect ambient, chilled and frozen groceries.
In a LinkedIn post, Christopher Evison, Senior Productivity Manager at Morrisons, said: “This is a great step forward for Click & Collect at Morrisons. It brings faster pickups - orders are pre-packed in paper bags and loaded into the lockers in advance. Simply enter your unique six-digit code when you arrive and go. And more flexibility - the lockers are helping us extend operating hours by two hours a day, giving customers even more options for when they collect. Freshness is guaranteed - the multi-temperature lockers can accommodate ambient, chilled and frozen products, whether customers are picking up a few essentials or their full weekly shop.”
He added: “There is also support when you need it - integrated VoCoVo headsets provide a direct two-way connection to store colleagues, making it easy to get assistance or complete any required ID checks."
"Huge thank you to all that have supported from both StrongPoint and Vocovo. It’s another great step forward in investing in our online proposition while keeping customer convenience at the heart of what we do. A huge well done to everyone involved in getting the launch over the line - a fantastic team effort. We’re really looking forward to seeing customers using the lockers and continuing to drive our online propostion forward.”
8. Currys ramps up social activity as it goes live on TikTok Shop
Currys has launched on TikTok Shop with a curated range of products, from health and beauty and coffee to seasonal and audio.
Building on the retailer’s TikTok activity, with its page having bagged over ten million ‘likes’, it will partner with content creators to showcase products to new audiences, and will host TikTok Live shopping events, bringing real-time product demos and instant purchasing to customers' feeds.
This will start as a trial in partnership with THG Commerce who will provide strategy, trading, shop management, weekly live streams and affiliate management services. As an official TikTok Shop partner, THG Commerce says it has generated over £44 million in GMV for its partners by providing a complete solution that covers everything from initial storefront setup and compliance to content creation, global fulfilment and customer services, managed under one roof.
9. Miniso set to replace HMV on London's Oxford Street with opening of 19,000 sq ft flagship store
Miniso is gearing up to open its first Miniso Land store in the UK. The 19,000 sq ft flagship will be located at 363 Oxford Street, London, currently occupied by HMV, and will line up alongside the retailer’s other flagship stores, which includes New York’s Times Square and Paris’s Champs-Élysées, alongside over 8,300 stores globally.
Sam Foyle, Co-head of Global Retail at Savills, which acted for the landlord, says: “We’re seeing continued interest from brands for space on Oxford Street. Pedestrianisation plans have really fuelled momentum over the past year and, as the street enters a more mature stage of recovery, we expect this appetite to continue.”
“Oxford Street is a microcosm of the UK high street, where brands are increasingly focused on creating memorable, experience led destinations. Miniso Land is a great example of that trend, bringing an innovative flagship concept to one of the world’s most recognisable retail locations. Its decision to open at 363 Oxford Street is a strong vote of confidence in London and reinforces Oxford Street’s appeal as a destination for ambitious global brands.”
A Miniso spokesperson says: “London is an important part of our international growth, and bringing Miniso Land to Oxford Street marks an exciting next step. The flagship reflects our long-term commitment to the UK and our ambition to connect people with the characters and stories they love and bring joy to everyday life.”
Earlier this month, HMV announced it intended to vacate the site in March 2027 after three years. It first launched the Oxford Street site in 1921 and reopened it in late 2023 following a four-year absence.
10. Tomáš Čupr bags $32 million for Duvo, an AI platform born from challenges he encountered while building Rohlik
Duvo, an automation platform that gives teams an AI workforce for their day-to-day operations, has announced a $32 million Series A led by Balderton Capital, with participation from existing investors Index Ventures, Northzone and Credo Ventures. The round brings its total funding to $48 million and will fund its expansion, starting with retailers and CPG companies.
Michael Green is also joining from Databricks as Senior Vice President, Go-to-Market. He previously served as a Senior Vice President at Salesforce. Spencer Insolia recently came onboard as Managing Director, US. He was previously President at Kmart and a Managing Director at Accenture. Christoph Schwaiger, former CEO at Aldi South Holdings, has also signed on as Senior Advisor for Europe.
"For a while I measured AI in heads, counting how many people an agent could replace. It's the wrong unit," says Tomáš Čupr, Co-founder and CEO at Duvo and Founder and Group CEO at Rohlik Group.
"At Rohlik, the gains I'd point to came from work nobody had the hours for. Our planners used to check about eight at-risk products a day per market for shortages. Now every signal gets checked, around the clock. We think of it as raising the GDP of every employee: more value from the people a company has, not the same value from fewer of them."

items.title: VoCoVo hires former Waterstones exec Emma Hillyard as CFO and former CBRE technology chief Paul Birkin as CTO
items.summary: Retail communications specialist, VoCoVo, has announced the appointments of Emma Hillyard as Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Paul Birkin as Chief Technology Officer (CTO).Hillyard has worked across both the private and not for profit sectors, including retail, with previous CFO roles at Waterstone
items.body:
Retail communications specialist, VoCoVo, has announced the appointments of Emma Hillyard as Chief Financial Officer (CFO) and Paul Birkin as Chief Technology Officer (CTO).
Hillyard has worked across both the private and not for profit sectors, including retail, with previous CFO roles at Waterstones, Blackwells and Alzheimer’s Society.
She says: “VoCoVo has achieved strong growth already, and my role is to help make sure we navigate this next period and build on the growth already seen. For me, that means giving teams the insight and support they need to make informed decisions and creating the right environment for people to do their best work."
"I’ve always been very people centric and believe culture is critical to making meaningful change stick. That was a big part of what attracted me to VoCoVo. Its people and culture are a real superpower, and I’m excited to build on that.”
Birkin has held C-suite positions at CBRE, Experian, Capita, Logica and Cisco.
He says, “I’ve spent much of my career leading large scale transformations where technology can make a visible difference. That’s what makes VoCoVo so exciting - there’s already a strong technology foundation and a true ambition to keep innovating. As retail becomes increasingly intelligent, AI has the potential to create huge business value. My focus is on turning that potential into tangible value for our customers and pushing what the connected store can deliver.”
Beth Worrall, CEO at VoCoVo, says: “Emma and Paul bring two highly complementary areas of expertise to VoCoVo. Emma helps ensure we have the right commercial foundations and insight to scale sustainably, while Paul helps us accelerate our technology roadmap and innovation to create greater impact for our customers."
"Just as importantly, they both share our focus on people, culture and creating meaningful, sustainable value. This is all critical to our next phase of growth, and I look forward to working with them as we build on the momentum we’ve already created.”

items.title: US grocery retailer Seed to Table enlists Live Buzz Intelligence for AI powered immersive in-store experience
items.summary: Seed to Table, a grocery retailer in Naples, Florida, has created Goldie, a conversational AI avatar who shoppers can talk to via a full size Proto Hologram screen.“Seed To Table is a cutting-edge grocery store/entertainment Mecca like no other and adding Goldie to it just brings us to another
items.body:
Seed to Table, a grocery retailer in Naples, Florida, has created Goldie, a conversational AI avatar who shoppers can talk to via a full size Proto Hologram screen.
“Seed To Table is a cutting-edge grocery store/entertainment Mecca like no other and adding Goldie to it just brings us to another level that no other supermarket has,” says Dan St. Martin, General Manager. "We are the Disney World of supermarkets.”
At the entrance, a seven-foot Proto Hologram presents information, advertising and Goldie, which has a face, voice and whimsical personality. Shoppers can ask Goldie questions, get recommendations and discover ideas. She can also remember preferences and previous interactions.
Throughout the store, participating brands use QR enabled shelf displays. Shoppers can scan to discover a brand story, learn about a product, receive an offer or recommendation, and explore content created specifically around what they’re seeing.
“Seed to Table deserves tremendous credit for having the vision to be first,” says James Beckmann, CEO at Live Buzz Intelligence. “They’re showing what is possible when a retailer modernises engagement at exactly the right moment. We’re excited to bring something genuinely new to shoppers.”
“”For years, we’ve been bringing people face-to-face with holograms in ways they never imagined possible,” says David Nussbaum, Founder and Chairman of Proto Hologram. “Now we’re bringing that same magic to something as ordinary as a trip to the grocery store. What excites me about this collaboration with Live Buzz Intelligence and Seed to Table is that we’re introducing new technology into retail which enhances the entire customer shopping experience."
"When a shopping cart has a personality, products can tell their own stories, and customers can interact with AI in real time, you’re getting a glimpse of what the future of retail looks like.”
Live Buzz Intelligence says that it plans to scale the model to thousands of retail locations across the US.

items.title: Morrisons AI specialist Mohsen Ghasempour hits the storefloor as retailer embraces advanced technology
items.summary: People working in technology need to spend more time where it is actually being used. So says Dr Mohsen Ghasempour, Chief AI Officer at Morrisons. Ghasempour recently joined the UK grocery retailer from Kingfisher. He has taken on overall responsibility for data and AI strategy, with a remit spanni
items.body:
People working in technology need to spend more time where it is actually being used. So says Dr Mohsen Ghasempour, Chief AI Officer at Morrisons.
Ghasempour recently joined the UK grocery retailer from Kingfisher. He has taken on overall responsibility for data and AI strategy, with a remit spanning customer growth, colleague empowerment, operational efficiency, manufacturing excellence and commercial excellence. He reports directly to Morrisons CEO Rami Baitiéh and took up the role on 1st October.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: "I cannot think of a better place to start understanding our business and shaping our AI and technology priorities than spending time with colleagues on the shopfloor."
He added: "Last week, I had the chance to spend time with Gordon Macpherson (Group Productivity Director) and Francesca Bezoari (Retail Support Office Director) in one of our stores, seeing some of the technology already in place, from electronic shelf labels to employing computer vision technology helping identify gaps on our shelves, and the infrastructure behind it all."
He concluded: "I have always believed that those of us working in technology need to spend more time where it is actually being used. Sometimes, seeing things first-hand helps you spot small opportunities that could save colleagues hours of work or make their day a little easier. Really encouraging to see how we are already embracing AI and advanced technology. With so much more we can do to make life easier for our colleagues and deliver better for our customers.

items.title: Many of Britain's best known brands are invisible when shoppers ask AI what to buy, Human Forward research
items.summary: AI assistants are becoming the place shoppers ask what to buy, and the next step, letting an AI agent buy for you, is already live for US shoppers in Gemini, Meta's Muse and Microsoft Copilot. Research published by Human Forward, a startup based out of London, shows most of Britain's best known bran
items.body:
AI assistants are becoming the place shoppers ask what to buy, and the next step, letting an AI agent buy for you, is already live for US shoppers in Gemini, Meta's Muse and Microsoft Copilot.
Research published by Human Forward, a startup based out of London, shows most of Britain's best known brands are not ready for this brave new world.
Human Forward asked six AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Google's Gemini, DeepSeek and Meta's Muse) the questions shoppers ask about 75 leading UK retailers and direct to consumer brands, and checked each brand's website for the standards AI agents use to find products and complete a purchase. It found:
Most brands can't be bought by an AI agent. Of the 50 sites it could check, 35 were not set up for an AI agent to buy from, including Marks and Spencer, Dunelm and Moonpig. The 15 that were ready all run on Shopify, which builds it in for its merchants. Brands on their own technology have been left to work it out alone.
One in five is never recommended. Asked for the best brands in their own category, no assistant named 15 of the 75 brands. Among the big retailers it was 12 of 50, including boohoo, New Look, Matalan, River Island, Schuh and AO.
The assistants disagree. When one assistant recommends a brand, on average 39% of the others leave it out. ChatGPT is the hardest to get into: it named a brand unprompted 40% of the time, against 60% for Claude.
Everyday names get lost. Ask an assistant “What is Iceland?” and all six describe the country, not the supermarket.
Being recommended is not being ready. Moonpig tops the table for AI answers at 99 out of 100, yet no agent checkout was found on its site.
Peter Abidi, Founder at Human Forward and formerly Digital Marketing and E-Commerce Director at Rapha, says: "AI shopping is arriving faster than most brands realise, and the brands most at risk aren't the small ones. They're the big names running their own technology, who have been left to work it out alone. Some of the most recommended brands in Britain still can't be bought by an agent."
"Some brands will decide they don't want agents buying for their customers, and that's their call. Being forgotten isn't. If your brand has an everyday name, assume the AI doesn't know it's you. Ask what Iceland is and you get the country. These are fixable problems, and most of the fixes are boring, but nobody fixes what they haven't measured."

items.title: The launch is now a broadcast: why retail brand moments are built for the screen
items.summary: Before the pandemic, about a fifth of UK retail sales happened online. In January 2021 that share hit 37.8%, and it has since settled at around 27%, according to the Office for National Statistics. The surge faded, but the shift stuck. A large share of shoppers now meet a product on a screen long be
items.body:
Before the pandemic, about a fifth of UK retail sales happened online. In January 2021 that share hit 37.8%, and it has since settled at around 27%, according to the Office for National Statistics.
The surge faded, but the shift stuck. A large share of shoppers now meet a product on a screen long before they meet it on a shelf.
That has changed what a product launch is for. The event in the room still matters, but it is no longer the whole point. For most retail brands, the launch has become a piece of content production, and the people who matter most are watching from somewhere else.
The audience is mostly not in the room
A launch used to be judged on who turned up: press, buyers, a few well-chosen faces. Now the real audience arrives through a livestream, a run of short-form clips, creator coverage and the product page that goes live the moment the reveal happens. The guests in the room are still important, but they are also the backdrop for footage that will be cut, captioned and pushed across channels for weeks afterwards.
That reframes the brief. The question is less "will the room enjoy it?" and more "will this look and sound right on a phone screen, in a feed, at a size of a few centimetres?"
What a broadcast ready launch needs
Retail teams that run launches like broadcasts tend to ask the same questions of a venue.
Can the cameras see it?Height matters more than floor space. A tall room lets lighting and screens sit above the audience, so cameras get clean sightlines to the stage without heads in the shot.
Can the light be controlled?Daylight is lovely and unpredictable. The best rooms offer both: natural light for the arrival and the drinks, full control once the cameras roll.
Does it all run from one place?Sound, lighting and video cues land better when a single operator controls them. A missed lighting cue is a small problem in the room and a large one on a livestream.
Is the AV built for broadcast?
If the footage is going out live or being edited into a campaign, the venue's screens and feeds need to be good enough to be filmed, not just watched.
Some venues have designed around exactly this. In King's Cross, the restored neo-classical civic building at spaces.townhall.co.uk pairs 13-metre ceilings in its main hall with 4K, broadcast-ready AV from Pixl Evolution, run from a single central control. It is the kind of setup that lets a brand film a launch to campaign standard without building a studio inside the room.
Treat the launch as a campaign asset
If the launch is content, it should be measured like content. That means planning the outputs before the event rather than after it. Decide which clips you need for which channels, how the livestream links through to a shoppable page, and which tracking will tie views to sales.
Retail technology makes this easier than it used to be. Livestream platforms can carry product links. Tagged URLs and QR codes on screen show which channels drove traffic. Basket data after the event shows whether interest turned into orders. The launch stops being a one-night cost and becomes a measurable piece of the marketing mix.
Location still does a lot of work
A broadcast launch still needs people in the room: press, partners, creators and the senior team. Getting them there easily is part of the job. Venues close to major transport hubs make attendance simpler, especially for guests travelling from outside London. A launch within minutes of King's Cross St Pancras, with its Underground, national rail and Eurostar connections, is within reach for guests coming from across the UK and from Europe.
The reveal is only the beginning
The most effective retail launches now treat the moment of reveal as the first frame of a much longer story. The room sets the tone, the cameras carry it, and the data shows what worked. Brands that plan for all three get far more from a single evening than a good night and a few photographs.

items.title: ‘The government needs to take us seriously’: Pub landlords brew plans to bar MPs – again
items.summary: Pub landlords across the country are poised to launch a fresh ban on hundreds of MPs after a campaign to cut VAT on hospitality fell on deaf ears in the House of Commons.  Andy Lennox, who led a ban on Labour MPs following the surge in business rates bills caused by last year’s Budget, told [...]
items.body:
‘The government needs to take us seriously’: Pub landlords brew plans to bar MPs – again
Pub landlords across the country are poised to launch a fresh ban on hundreds of MPs after a campaign to cut VAT on hospitality fell on deaf ears in the House of Commons.
Andy Lennox, who led a ban on Labour MPs following the surge in business rates bills caused by last year’s Budget, told City AM landlords are on the verge of launching a new movement to bar politicians.
He said any new action, which would include thousands of pubs across the UK, would ban every MP who has not shown public support to a cut for VAT for hospitality firms.
Lennox said: ”There is so much anger out in the industry at the moment and following the Budget there have been a number of comments made by Treasury ministers and actions by the Chancellor that just show there is zero respect for our industry and for what we do.”
Pub, bar and restaurant bosses had been urging the government to halve VAT to 10 per cent in a campaign led by celebrity chef Tom Kerridge.
But John Healey opted not to heed these calls at last week’s Budget. Instead, he confirmed an already-announced 20 per cent cut to pubs’ business rates and hiked alcohol duty by 2p on every pint.
Lennox added: “The government needs to take us seriously and seemingly lobbying MPs and having the support for a VAT cut line with Europe of nearly 300 of them isn’t cutting through – further action is required.”
354 MPs could be barred
If Hospitality Voices, the group of pub landlords led by Lennox, goes ahead with a new ban, 354 MPs could find themselves barred from their local.
The group’s tracker shows that these hundreds of MPs, including Andy Burnham and John Healey, have failed to back a cut to VAT while 296 have shown support.
The hospitality sector’s anger towards the Labour government was further fuelled over the weekend, when Treasury minister Emma Reynolds said that employers are “not working people” as she tried to justify tax hikes.
Lennox, who runs several pubs in Dorset and Hampshire, said: “Emma Reynolds’ comments are an insult to everyone who has built a business and created jobs. If this is how the Treasury sees employers, it explains its extraordinary disconnect from business.”
Pub bosses will decide next week whether to launch a new ban on MPs. It is hoped that this new campaign could garner more bipartisan support because it is not targeted at one political party.
Last December, pub landlords’ decision to ban Labour MPs from their premises eventually resulted in a £300m business rates relief package being handed out by then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves.

items.title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
items.summary: After a second apparent cyber-attack in weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned , their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F). The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. Continue reading...
items.body: 1:15 'It's a form of terrorism': fridges across Europe hit by suspected cyber-attacks – video Explainer Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? After a second apparent cyber-attack in weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F). The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean? The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia. It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software. Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack. View image in fullscreen Workers at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, dispose of spoiled food. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPA This is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control. Who is doing it? No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay – which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat. “The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos. The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea is believed to have been behind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame. Western intelligence chiefs say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months. Discerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”. How is it possible? The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates. Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges? Read more Nick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to install patches is they can take time to run, which leaves periods when machinery needs to be offline – an obvious problem for food retailers. But he said a simpler explanation could be that the people running the fridges are not aware of the problem, “don’t think about that and it’s not top of their agenda”. In Monday’s wave of incidents, Coop in Sweden said some of its fridges were linked to a 4G mobile network that made them more exposed. ICA said its system was provided by Danfoss, the Danish company that had problems in France. What can shops do to defend themselves? The simple answer is to patch their software systems. According to the Belgian refrigerator group Sabcobel, the impact of Monday’s hack could have been far worse if they had not started patching fridges after the 12 October attack in France. In the UK, which has not yet been affected, retailers are “currently working with the National Cyber Security Centre(NCSC) to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks” said Graham Wynn, the assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium. Why have British supermarkets not been hit yet? Internet-exposed refrigeration systems are most popular in countries including France, Italy, Greece and Belgium, according to the cybersecurity company Forescout. Daniel dos Santos, its vice president of research, said: “When we checked the data for these exposed systems online of supermarkets, the UK is not in the top 10.” He said the risk was not negligible, but “I wouldn’t say it’s super-high right now for the UK specifically”. A spokesperson for the NCSC said it was “working with its international partners and industry to fully understand details of an incident”. items.title: Private equity under fire as crisis at Poundland leaves 12,000 jobs at risk before Christmas
items.summary: The crisis at Poundland has sparked fresh concern over private equity ownership of British high street brands as the budget chain teeters on the brink of collapse.
items.body:
Private equity under fire as crisis at Poundland leaves 12,000 jobs at risk before Christmas
The crisis at Poundland has sparked fresh concern over private equity ownership of British high street brands as the budget chain teeters on the brink of collapse.
Poundland, which was bought by Gordon Brothers for £1 last year, looks set to crash into administration this week, putting 600 stores and 12,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas.
Politicians and retail veterans said the demise of the company exposes a worrying trend that has seen private equity vultures prey on household names across Britain.
The row comes amid warnings that private equity has ransacked the London stock market – with figures from City broker Peel Hunt showing more than 100 UK-listed firms have been snapped up by such buyout groups in the past five years.
Gordon Brothers has rejected a rescue bid for Poundland – sparking fears it is trying to sell the group off piecemeal rather than secure its future.
Labour MP Liam Byrne, who is chairman of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said: ‘There is this wider question of whether this is yet another bit of the British high street that has been overloaded with debt in an unsustainable way by venture capitalists.’
Poundland is nearing collapse after its owners rejected a bid for the brand
Calling on the Government to convene talks in a bid to save Poundland from collapse, he added: ‘Ministers have got to move pretty sharpish today to understand whether 12,000 British jobs are about to be sacrificed so that an American investment house can have a bumper Christmas.
‘This is three times as many jobs as British Steel that are at stake. You’ve got creditors and suppliers all depending on a rescue and you’ve got this thick layer of mystery around Poundland that we’ve got to cut through.’
Poundland, which filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last week, closed around 200 shops as part of a sweeping restructuring under the US investment house.
The business started to rebound but Gordon Brothers put the retailer up for sale in September and has since rejected a bid that would have saved the whole company and its 600 stores.
It has fuelled concerns that the private equity firm is pushing Poundland towards administration despite receiving a bid from Martin Property Group that was backed by Poundland’s management.
The Northern Irish firm reportedly refused to meet demands for an upfront repayment of a £30million shareholder loan, which Gordon Brothers inherited from previous owners Pepco.
That means the 36-year-old retailer’s brand and its shops will not be sold as a whole, leading to a break-up of Poundland – and meaning jobs are at risk at any shop not bought.
Byrne told the BBC: ‘I’m afraid we have seen a pattern of behaviour now from private equity at Morrisons, Asda, WH Smith, Body Shop, where they’re basically geared up to the nines, overburdened with debt and its workers and high streets and consumers that end up paying the price when it all goes wrong.’
Poundland's failure would mark one of the biggest High Street collapses since Debenhams closed its doors in 2021 with the loss of 12,000 jobs.
Andy Higginson, former Poundland director, said he was ‘not entirely surprised’ by the crisis at the retailer.
He told the BBC: ‘Often particularly through the private equity cycle, good businesses can end up with bad balance sheets and that may be the case here. The situation we face is a tricky one in that the owners interests and what we the public might consider the business’ interests, can be different.’
Ministers have signalled that they are ready to take action, with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds last week demanding answers from Gordon Brothers and instructing officials to establish the facts.
Over the weekend, Reform UK Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick accused Gordon Brothers of ‘crony capitalism’ and called on the government to ensure Poundland ‘is not stripped for parts by its American owners’.
And Steve Smith, founder of Poundland, estimated 30,000 jobs were at risk because the retailer’s ‘suppliers will suffer or be at risk of going into administration.’
He said: ‘If Poundland goes into administration the suppliers will get next to nothing in the pound they are owed and 12,000 people will lose their jobs, the only people that will make a lot of money out of this will be the liquidators.’
The City has already sounded the alarm on the raid of listed British firms by private equity, with 131 firms taken private since 2021, according to figures from Peel Hunt.
Higginson said businesses had fallen into private equity hands as banks failed to cater to small and medium-sized firms, with the stock market ‘a shadow of its former self’.

items.title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
items.summary: Chains in at least seven countries say fridge temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French stores Europe live – latest updates Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in dozens of their stores soared overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of losses in France. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been victims of a cyberattack. Continue reading...
items.body:
Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in dozens of their stores soared overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of losses in France.
Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been victims of a cyberattack.
The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of the cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks in the wake of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
An ICA store at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed.”
The head of the national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it was working on incidents around Sweden. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last month reported a similar incident to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and freezers in dozens of its supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg had been hit.
It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a store north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”
A company spokesperson, Sarah De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected stores, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”
He told the Belga news agency the incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their stores respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 stores.
“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons store to rise suddenly.
Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to remove some food products from refrigeration units as a precaution and expected some food waste as a result.
In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said stores operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local stores had been affected.
At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.
Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, SuperValu, said refrigeration systems limited to a specific model in 13 of its 223 stores had been affected by a cyber-incident, and that chilled and frozen products had been removed from sale.
Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.
“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.
Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had knownand as yet unfixed flaws, he said.
“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he said. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”
In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.
The stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.
The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.

items.title: Can Marks & Spencer’s TikTok star help it ‘dump the frump’?
items.summary: Marks & Spencer will face shareholders on Wednesday, with hopes of presenting a lift from its breakout social media star, Kathryn Turner, writes Felix Armstrong. Ditch the fake blood and vampire fangs: Britain’s viral Halloween costume this year featured a white shirt, a blue sweater vest and a blonde wig. Kathryn Turner, Marks & Spencer’s [...]
items.body:
Can Marks & Spencer’s TikTok star help it ‘dump the frump’?
Marks & Spencer will face shareholders on Wednesday, with hopes of presenting a lift from its breakout social media star, Kathryn Turner, writes Felix Armstrong.
Ditch the fake blood and vampire fangs: Britain’s viral Halloween costume this year featured a white shirt, a blue sweater vest and a blonde wig. Kathryn Turner, Marks & Spencer’s director of product development, has become a runaway social media star in recent months, and the retailer has quickly capitalised on her newfound Tiktok fame.
Turner, dubbed this year’s top ‘gay Halloween’ costume, has soared in popularity in recent months after taking her followers inside M&S Food’s latest products, including candyfloss-flavoured grapes and chocolate and pistachio sandwiches.
Since relaunching her social media profiles in May, Turner has garnered 281,000 followers on Instagram and a further 319,000 on TikTok, far more than the official M&S Food channel’s 270,000. She has worked at the retailer since 1995, and her breakthrough food creation was Tubby Toast, inspired by the children’s TV show Teletubbies, which first hit the shelves in 1998.
But M&S’s latest social media star, whose fans include Nigella Lawson and Ian Wright, is not alone. The retailer has encouraged its staff to grow their individual profiles online, and the company says its employees run about 600 Facebook pages and 100 TikTok accounts offering viewers the inside scoop on its products.
Richard Hyman, an independent retail analyst, said Kathryn Turner’s online profile has “clearly a very successful campaign” for the company.
M&S Food is “performing very strongly and gaining market share,” he added. “It’s always a mistake to equate social media success with commercial progress, but this will have played its part.”
The grocer notched 10.7 per cent sales growth in the four weeks to October, according to the latest NIQ data. The analytics firm attributed this boost directly to Turner’s online presence.
“M&S’ strong performance has been supported by growing social media interest in its product launches, with director of product development Kathryn Turner attracting attention on TikTok, reflecting the retailer’s ability to turn product buzz into shopper demand,” NIQ’s data experts said.
Clothing arm in need of a lift
Marks & Spencers has long been pushing to widen its Gen-Z audience after hiring Maddy Evans, formerly of Topshop, in 2023. The retailer hopes to provide more proof when it publishes its first-half results on Wednesday.
At the company’s annual general meeting this summer, chief executive Stuart Machin told shareholders that the retailer has worked hard to develop its offering for younger customers, through collaborations with influencers like Amelia Dimoldenberg, declaring that it has successfully “dumped the frump”.
The retailer celebrated its 100th anniversary in July by staging a catwalk show at London Fashion Week, in the latest sign that M&S is finally becoming cool. But Machin has reassured investors that he will not stray too far from the middle-class families which have long propped up the brand, saying his mother had reminded him its clothes were at risk of becoming “too skimpy”.
Hyman cautioned, however, that Turner’s efforts are mainly benefitting M&S’ food arm, while its clothing and home businesses are “finding life more challenging,” despite these efforts to dump the frump.
This side of the company has been slower to recover from the cyber attack which ravaged the retailer in April last year, knocking £131m from its balance sheet. Sales in food, home and beauty fell by 7.7 per cent in the year to March, while food sales jumped by seven per cent.
The retailer told shareholders in May that its non-food arm was worse hit by the “temporary pause in online trading and systems access, which disrupted stock flow and restricted availability”.
But analysts said M&S has made solid progress since last year’s cyberattack, and its share price has gained nearly 30 per cent in the last six months. As it tries to bring its clothing business up to speed with its food arm, the retailer may have benefited from a surge in sales of white shirts and blonde wigs this Halloween.

items.title: Cadbury filled eggs return in time for Easter 2027 head start
items.summary: Cadbury is urging retailers to get a head start in the run-up to Easter 2027 with the return of its filled eggs range. Brand owner Mondelēz International says seasonal sales continue to play a crucial role for convenience retailers, with 72% saying they are very… This story continues at Cadbury filled eggs return in time for Easter 2027 head start Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Brand owner Mondelēz International says seasonal sales continue to play a crucial role for convenience retailers, with 72% saying they are very important to their business.
“With Easter 2027 bringing a more compressed season, planning across the full Easter trading period is key,” the company says.
The sales opportunity taps into occasions including, self-eat, sharing, egg hunts and gifting, with Easter being the second biggest season for retail performance after Christmas, it adds.
The Cadbury filled egg range includes:
- Cadbury Creme Egg (40g, RRP 85p)
- Cadbury Biscoff Filled Egg (32g, RRP 85p)
According to Mondelēz, the average shopper buys four filled eggs across the Easter season, “emphasising the importance of strong availability and visibility in-store from the beginning of the Easter sales period in November.”
Its “How You Eat Yours” consumer campaign runs from January to March and its retailer competition “How Do You Display Yours?” is back from this month (November).
Exclusive to independent convenience retailers, the competition invites them to share their most innovative and eye-catching Cadbury Creme Egg displays for the chance to win £1,000 for the best display.
In addition, every display submitted will enter retailers into a prize draw, with one lucky retailer per month from November to February winning £1,000.
To enter the competition, retailers can visit SnackDisplay.co.uk, Mondelēz International’s trade website.
Sarah Walker, brand manager for Cadbury Creme Egg at Mondelēz International, said: “We are excited to kick off the Easter season with a Cadbury Creme Egg campaign that will look to drive footfall into stores.
“Cadbury Creme Egg is the signpost of the Easter season, and we know shoppers have their own individual ways of enjoying it.
“Our ‘Admit How You Eat Yours’ campaign really allows us to ignite the Easter conversation and bring that individuality to life in a light-hearted way.”

items.title: Poundland's former owner offers to invest as minister prepares to meet board
items.summary: Wolverhampton's Steve Smith says he attempted to contact Gordon Brothers but did not get a reply.
items.body:
Poundland's former owner offers to invest in firm
- Published
Poundland's former owner has said he would invest in the firm as a government minister said she would meet the firm's board.
Steve Smith, who founded the Walsall-based business, leaving it in 2006, said he had attempted to contact owners Gordon Brothers having been "really surprised" to learn about them filing for administration when sales were up 11% on last year.
The BBC understands that Business Minister Kate Dearden will meet with senior Poundland executives later this week to discuss the company's threatened insolvency.
US-based Gordon Brothers said it was evaluating interest for the whole business and formal and indicative offers for significant viable parts of it.
Gordon Brothers, who bought the firm from Polish retail group Pepco last year for Â£1, has stopped funding the business and rejected a takeover offer from Irish firm Martin Property Group (MPG).
The retailer has given the business until Thursday to find a rescue deal, putting up to 12,000 staff at risk.
It's understood the meeting with Deardon will be predominantly a "fact finding" meeting with government sources conceding there is limited scope for the government to intervene in a commercial transaction albeit one that puts over 10,000 jobs and hundreds of stores at risk.
The meeting was first reported by Sky News.
There is no current meeting planned between the government and executives from current owners, US private equity group Gordon Brothers.
Concerns have been raised that Gordon Brothers have declined an offer from another buyer to keep Poundland afloat in order to ensure repayment of Â£30 million loan it inherited after buying the company for Â£1.
More on Poundland
- 'Poundland closure would leave a void in our town' 
  - Published2 days ago
- How Poundland grew from a market stall to a high street giant 
  - Published3 days ago
- Poundland staff protest after chain approach administrators 
  - Published3 days ago
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government was "ready to support" staff as he also called for answers over why an offer to buy the business had been rejected.
Smith, from Wolverhampton and who set up the firm in 1990 with a store in Burton-upon-Trent, Staffordshire, said he contacted the owners over the last three months but had no reply. He had thought that was good news as he assumed the firm must have had offers on the table.
"And maybe I was a bit too late, but I'd certainly... with talking to the staff and how Poundland's performing at the moment, I'd certainly, if there's an opportunity, I definitely want to put some money back in there."
He said he was still in touch with staff there at levels within the business and "even last week" sales were 11.2 % upon last year.
"Although Poundland made a loss last year, they're going to make a good profit this year, so it's just crazy."
He warned that the two or three thousand suppliers to the firm only worked for Poundland so they would be directly affected by its collapse.
"This is not just about 12, 000 jobs. I'm estimating more like 20 or 30,000 jobs," he added.
The company has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, and Smith said it had between four and five million customers a week, so with Poundland not being present on high streets would "cause a lot of other retailers to fall as well".
Liam Byrne, chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee and Labour MP for Birmingham Hodge Hill and Solihull North, said he felt the company could be saved and "the whole deal stinks to high heaven right now".
"Because I think the issue that we've got is, you've got an owner that could well be trying to cut and run, to sell a business that is in fact a going concern in order to maximize their own profits and put in jeopardy 12,000 British jobs on the high street."
'Get on the case now'
"Our message today to government and to ministers is, do not leave this to the last minute, which is Thursday... please get on the case now to get everybody around the table to maximize every option to save as much of the business as possible," he added.
In a statement, the board of Poundland Limited said it had been "working on a formal sale process for Poundland" and despite "enormous efforts it had not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole".
"We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment."
Gordon Brothers said: "While Martin Property Group had been identified as the preferred bidder by Poundland's management team, attention must now turn to other active bids."
The interest, formal and indicative offers were being evaluated "with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland's people and all relevant stakeholders."

The company, which now has 18 petrol stations and convenience stores across the north of England and Birmingham, wants the Canal Road forecourt to become one of its leading sites.
Canal Road has a range of food-to-go options, with Spar’s £4.50-or-less meal deal in-store alongside a sit-in Subway and two Costa Coffee machines.

“The store is designed to accommodate the evolving needs of the local community as well as support through traffic.
“We have incorporated an extensive offering with special promotions running to ensure that all customers enjoy their experience when they visit Canal Road.”

items.title: Sixty seven per cent of shoppers will trade delivery speed for lower costs
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Retailers investing in AI ahead of Peak 2026 risk focusing on operational efficiencies while overlooking the delivery fundamentals that matter most to shoppers, according to new research from Scurri. Two studies of UK retailers and consumers show businesses accelerating their use of AI to tackle rising costs and increasingly complex customer journeys. But shoppers want […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Retailers investing in AI ahead of Peak 2026 risk focusing on operational efficiencies while overlooking the delivery fundamentals that matter most to shoppers, according to new research from Scurri.
Two studies of UK retailers and consumers show businesses accelerating their use of AI to tackle rising costs and increasingly complex customer journeys. But shoppers want to keep delivery affordable, be told when their order will arrive and get communications quickly when something goes wrong.
64% of consumers worry retailers are using AI mainly to reduce costs. Among retailers, business efficiency is one of the leading reasons for AI adoption, cited by 32%.
Yet shoppers appear less interested in the technology than the outcome. When waiting for an order, 53% say real-time tracking matters most and 44% prioritise an accurate delivery date. Almost half (47%) would accept a Peak order arriving late if they had been warned in advance.
The findings also challenge the assumption that Peak shoppers demand even faster fulfilment. Free delivery matters to 61%, compared with 29% prioritising next day delivery and just 13% same day. Two thirds (67%) would accept longer delivery times during Peak in return for free or cheaper delivery.
The Peak battleground may therefore be shifting from speed towards certainty and value. Retailers are looking to AI to help deliver this. Almost six in ten (58%) say they are likely to use automated AI to manage ecommerce delivery strategy and carrier operations, while retailers estimate AI automation of carrier management could reduce delivery costs by an average of 10.6%.
AI could also help address problems before they reach the customer; 33% of retailers see potential in predicting and preventing failed deliveries, while 31% identify monitoring delivery issues and carrier performance.
Consumers want AI but they also want control. Some 60% would be likely to use an AI agent capable of resolving a delivery problem, such as finding a parcel, rearranging delivery or organising a refund or replacement. However, 88% say they should always have the option to speak to a human and 85% want to know when they are interacting with AI. 31% do not believe AI would improve their delivery experience at all.
Rory O’Connor, Scurri founder and CEO, said, “Peak is going to provide a reality check for retail AI. Retailers understandably want AI to reduce costs and complexity, but shoppers don’t care about the technology, they want to know whether delivery is affordable, whether it arrives when promised and whether someone takes responsibility when things go wrong.”
“The opportunity is to use AI to make the delivery promise more intelligent, by selecting the right carrier, identifying potential failures before they happen and giving retailers and customers better visibility.”
